title: Work and Trades
objective: After this level you can describe the work of farmers, builders and craftsmen.
summary: Nearly all Egyptians farmed, while skilled craftspeople worked beside them and were paid in rations. The Satire of the Trades mocked every job except the scribe’s.

cards.headline: An Egyptian father’s advice: be a scribe, since every other job is miserable.
cards.body: Egyptologists call it the Satire of the Trades, and New Kingdom students copied it as a writing exercise. It’s a biased guide to Egyptian work, and a very vivid one.

cards.headline: The Satire of the Trades
cards.body: In this text, a father walks his son to scribal school and mocks every other job on the way. The potter is covered with earth. The barber wears out his arms. The fisherman works among crocodiles. The washerman handles other people’s filth. It probably dates to the Middle Kingdom, and students kept copying it for centuries after. Career counseling, Egyptian style: scare the kid into studying.

cards.headline: Most people farmed
cards.body: The jokes hide a plain fact: nearly all Egyptians worked the land and were probably tied to it. In theory all land belonged to the king, though people living on it couldn’t easily be removed, and some land could be bought and sold. So most Egyptians lived by Level 4’s farming year: Akhet’s flood, Peret’s plowing and sowing, Shemu’s harvest. The river set everyone’s work calendar.

cards.headline: Craft and pay
cards.body: Craftspeople worked alongside the farmers, and Britannica says they raised their techniques, many first borrowed from Asia, to extraordinary levels of perfection. With no coins, pay often came as food rations, just as Level 52 described. As for the Satire, some Egyptologists doubt “satire” is even the right word, because its pictures of hard labor are so starkly realistic. The joke may have been truer than it was funny.

mascot.line: Every job has a bad side. This text just wrote them all down in one place.

questions.prompt: In the Satire of the Trades, which career does the father want for his son?

options.label: Potter
options.rationale: The potter is mocked for being covered with earth.

options.label: Fisherman
options.rationale: The fisherman is mocked for working among crocodiles.

options.label: Barber
options.rationale: The barber is mocked for wearing out his arms.

questions.explanation: The father is taking his son to scribal school and mocks every other job.

questions.prompt: Why is the Satire of the Trades a biased guide to Egyptian jobs?

options.label: It was written by foreign visitors
It mocks other jobs to persuade a boy to become a scribe
It only describes the pharaoh’s palace
options.rationale: It covers potters, barbers, fishermen and more.

options.label: It was written a thousand years after Egypt fell
options.rationale: It probably dates to the Middle Kingdom.

questions.explanation: It’s a father’s sales pitch for the scribe’s life, so every other job looks as bad as possible.

questions.prompt: Nearly all Egyptians worked the land. From Level 4, in which season did they bring in the harvest?

options.label: Peret
options.rationale: Peret was for plowing and sowing.

options.label: Deshret
options.rationale: Deshret was the red desert, not a season.

questions.explanation: Shemu, the season of low water, was harvest time.
